framework.name: Minto SCQA
framework.one_liner: Frames a problem statement as Situation, Complication, Question and Answer, so that the audience arrives at the main point already holding the question that the point answers.

slots.label: Situation
slots.description: The stable, agreed baseline: what the audience already knows and accepts about the subject, stated so that nobody argues with it.

slots.label: Complication
slots.description: What happened in that situation to disturb it: something changed, broke, arrived or fell short, and created the need to act.

slots.label: Question
slots.description: The single question the complication raises in the audience's mind. In speech it is almost never asked out loud, and when a question is asked out loud it is usually not this one.

slots.label: Answer
slots.description: The governing thought that resolves the question: a point, not a topic. It sits at the top of the pyramid and immediately raises the next question.

relations.label: disrupted by
relations.description: the stable situation is disrupted by the complication

relations.label: raises
relations.description: raises the question in the audience's mind: normally the complication, though the answer raises the next one

relations.label: answered by
relations.description: the question is answered by the answer, the governing thought

relations.label: elaborates
relations.description: one statement adds detail to another statement in the same slot

examples.title: The memo about the sales force
examples.summary: Minto's introduction pattern in its everyday habitat: a division head writes to a board that already accepts the baseline, states the two changes that broke it, and opens with a point rather than a topic. The question is never written down, because the reader is already asking it.

source.title: Fielding Instruments: the memo to the board
source.attribution: Written for this page in the pattern of Barbara Minto, The Pyramid Principle (1987): the S-C-Q-A introduction of a business memo.
source.text: Fielding Instruments has sold its laboratory instruments through a direct field sales force for the past ten years. Everyone on the board already knows this, and nobody disputes it: the eighty-person field force has been the division's main advantage over the distributors it competes with. Since the board last reviewed the channel, two things have changed. The division's twenty largest customers have moved their purchasing onto an online marketplace that the field force does not serve, and the cost of a single field visit has doubled. The division head has to write the board a memo. She does not head it 'some thoughts on the sales force'. She writes: the division should stop selling through the field force alone and put half of the sales budget behind the marketplace channel within twelve months. Nowhere in the memo does she put the question on the page. She does not have to; by the time the board reaches her sentence, it is already asking it.

nodes.label: Ten years of direct field selling
nodes.text: For the past ten years the division has sold its laboratory instruments through a direct field sales force.
nodes.source_quote: has sold its laboratory instruments through a direct field sales force for the past ten years

nodes.label: The force is the main advantage
nodes.text: The eighty-person field force has been the division's main advantage over the distributors it competes with.
nodes.source_quote: the eighty-person field force has been the division's main advantage over the distributors it competes with

nodes.label: The board already accepts this
nodes.text: The baseline is common ground rather than an argument: everyone on the board already knows it and nobody disputes it.
nodes.source_quote: Everyone on the board already knows this, and nobody disputes it

nodes.label: Top customers moved to marketplace
nodes.text: The division's twenty largest customers have moved their purchasing onto an online marketplace that the field force does not serve.
nodes.source_quote: The division's twenty largest customers have moved their purchasing onto an online marketplace that the field force does not serve

nodes.label: Cost of a field visit has doubled
nodes.text: The cost of a single field visit has doubled.
nodes.source_quote: the cost of a single field visit has doubled

nodes.label: The force is now a shrinking asset
nodes.text: Taken together the two changes turn the field force from the division's advantage into a shrinking asset: dearer per call and blind to the accounts that matter most.
nodes.rationale: The scenario states the two changes separately; that they compound - a channel costing twice as much per call while the largest buyers leave it - is the reading that makes the situation a complication rather than two unrelated facts.

nodes.label: What to do about the channel?
nodes.text: The question the board is already asking and the memo never writes: what should the division do about its route to market?
nodes.rationale: Sentence 8 says the question is never put on the page, and the complication leaves exactly one open decision - what to do about the channel - which the answer in sentence 7 addresses directly, so the question is nearly forced by the stated facts.

nodes.label: How, without losing the accounts?
nodes.text: The new question the answer itself raises, and the point where the pyramid under the introduction begins: how do you move half the budget without losing the accounts the field force holds?
nodes.rationale: Minto's rule is that the answer becomes the next question in the reader's mind (why? or how?). The scenario states the commitment but nothing about execution, so the follow-on question is a structural inference, not a reading of the text.

nodes.label: Stop relying on the force alone
nodes.text: The memo's governing thought, stated as a point rather than a topic: the division should stop selling through the field force alone.
nodes.source_quote: the division should stop selling through the field force alone

nodes.label: Half the budget to the marketplace
nodes.text: Half of the sales budget goes behind the marketplace channel within twelve months.
nodes.source_quote: put half of the sales budget behind the marketplace channel within twelve months

edges.source_quote: Since the board last reviewed the channel, two things have changed
Since the board last reviewed the channel, two things have changed

edges.rationale: The advantage named in sentence 2 is exactly what the two changes erode.

edges.source_quote: Everyone on the board already knows this, and nobody disputes it: the eighty-person field force has been the division's main advantage

edges.rationale: Losing the largest buyers from the only channel forces the channel question.
A doubled cost per visit makes the same question a budget question.
The compounded reading is what makes the question urgent rather than routine.
Sentence 7 is a direct answer to the unwritten question and to nothing else in the scenario.
Minto's introduction hands off to the pyramid: the answer raises the next question.

edges.source_quote: the division should stop selling through the field force alone and put half of the sales budget behind the marketplace channel within twelve months

examples.title: Poseidon: from a hundred-year-old freight market to flying boats
examples.summary: David Zagaynov narrates a complete SCQA on air: logistics unchanged for a hundred years, then two things that changed (the Soviet ekranoplan's blockers dissolved by composites and modern controls, and ground-effect craft falling under the Coast Guard rather than the FAA), then the governing thought - so what we're building are flying boats.

source.episode_title: xAI merges with X, Isomorphic Labs raises $600M (Aaron Levie, Alexis Ohanian, RJ Halperin, Cristobal Valenzuela, David Zagaynov, Sam Lessin)

examples.why_this_episode: The founder tells the whole introduction in one contiguous passage, so the Situation, the Complication and the Answer are all quotable facts. Two questions are asked out loud in that passage and neither is the one the answer answers, which is exactly the provenance point this framework exists to make: the Minto question has to be derived even when a transcript is full of question marks.

nodes.label: Logistics unchanged for 100 years
nodes.text: Logistics has been a market largely unchanged for the past hundred years; it is where the founders started looking.
nodes.source_quote: And so we were, I think ideating about like logistics and aerospace and I think like logistics, especially has been a market that's been largely unchanged for the past hundred years.

nodes.label: Same planes, same hub-and-spoke
nodes.text: The same 737s and Cessnas still fly the freight, and ship cargo is containerised on a hub-and-spoke model.
nodes.source_quote: The types of planes that we're flying are like largely the same, same 737, same like Cessna's and on the ship cargo side has been pretty much like containerized cargo with very much like spoken hub model.

nodes.label: Soviet ekranoplans, 60s and 70s
nodes.text: Ekranoplans were built in the Soviet Union in the 1960s and 70s and were at the time the highest cargo-capacity planes ever built: flying ships.
nodes.source_quote: So Echronoplaans were like types of vehicles that were built in the Soviet Union in the 60s and 70s. And at the time they were like the highest cargo capacity, like planes ever built, like they're like flying ships essentially.

nodes.label: Ground effect: lift-drag +30-50%
nodes.text: Flying in ground effect, extremely close to the water, cuts drag and adds lift: an increase in the lift-to-drag ratio of 30 to 50 percent.
nodes.source_quote: A largely reduces your drag and it increases your lift. So you can carry a lot more and spend a lot less fuel. So it's like increase of your lift drag ratio by 30 to 50%.

nodes.label: Soviet-era blockers now solved
nodes.text: In the modern age most of the problems the Soviets had are solved: it was a controls problem and a materials-science problem, and composites answer the second.
nodes.source_quote: the really crazy thing about ground effect vehicles in the modern age is like a lot of the problems that the Soviets had are solved for the most part. So it's really done a controls issue and a material science problem and composites are incredible material science.

nodes.label: Coast Guard certifies, not FAA
nodes.text: Ground-effect vehicles are not regulated by the FAA but by the Coast Guard, and Coast Guard certification is significantly easier.
nodes.source_quote: And so but the really cool thing is like the ground fake vehicles are not regulated by the FAA, they're regulated by the Coast Guard. And so Coast Guard certification is significantly easier than FAA.

nodes.label: FAA path: a decade, no flights
nodes.text: Companies that built eVTOL aircraft IPO'd or SPAC'd for billions without ever flying a commercial flight, because FAA certification takes a decade or more.
nodes.source_quote: So you have like really great companies that have built cool like EV toll stuff and like they've IPO'd or SPAC'd or whatever for billions of dollars, but they've never actually had a commercial flight because the FA regulatory process is so long. So it's like a decade plus to get certified.

nodes.label: Composites matured in 10-15 years
nodes.text: Composites have come into their own over the past ten to fifteen years with good manufacturing nearby; Poseidon buys all of its composites from ATV Composites.
nodes.source_quote: Like composites are really coming to their own in the past 10, 15 years in some terms of being able to, actually very good, there's very good manufacturing here. So like, ATV composites is where we get all of ours, and that's in the labor more.

nodes.label: Hobbyist RC parts got very good
nodes.text: As gamer GPUs enabled machine learning, hobbyist-grade RC hardware has become extremely good: motors, electronic systems and sensors small enough to fit on the aircraft.
nodes.source_quote: And so then like on the electronic side, I think like there's in the same way that like GPUs for like gamers like enabled machine learning, they're just like the hobbyist grade RC stuff has gotten extremely good. And so just like really move forward like the quality of motors available, the quality of like electronic systems, sensors, the types of sensors that are available right now have gone small enough that we can fit them on here.

nodes.label: Regulatory arbitrage in hard tech
nodes.text: A host names the pattern on air: regulatory arbitrage, previously the domain of crypto, is now being used in hard tech.
nodes.source_quote: A good Regarb just gets you going. It's previously the domain of crypto stuff, but now in hard tech, we're taking advantage of Regarb.

nodes.label: Constraint: physics to paperwork
nodes.text: The binding constraint on coastal and island air freight is no longer aerodynamics or materials but the cost and duration of certification.
nodes.rationale: c1 says the physics and materials problems are solved while c2 and c3 say certification is what keeps well-funded competitors from ever flying commercially; taken together the blocking constraint has moved from the vehicle to the regulator.

nodes.label: What could we build to disrupt it?
nodes.text: The founders' own question, voiced in the narration: what could they build to disrupt a logistics market that had not changed in a hundred years?
nodes.source_quote: And so we were going through a bunch of ideas of like what we could build to disrupt this,

nodes.label: Why now and not decades ago?
nodes.text: A host asks the why-now question: what in the regulatory picture and in the tech tree has enabled this now rather than decades ago?
nodes.source_quote: The question is really just like why now but I want like more of a breakdown of like all the different things from the regulatory to the tech tree that's enabled this to happen now and not earlier because at the same time like this feels like something that could have happened decades ago but why are we just why are we just breaking through with this now?

nodes.label: Cheapest way to move coastal cargo?
nodes.text: The question the complication actually forces and nobody asks: now that ground effect works and the craft can be certified as a boat, what is the cheapest way to move freight along coasts and between islands?
nodes.rationale: Minto's question is the one the complication raises in the listener's mind, and it is never spoken here. c1 (the physics is solved), c2 (a cheaper certifier already has jurisdiction) and c7 fix it almost completely: the only variable left open is the vehicle, which is exactly what a1 answers.
nodes.idea: Coastal and island freight is an underserved lane where a boat-certified ground-effect craft undercuts air freight by three to four times on price per kilogram-mile.

nodes.label: Which markets can switch regulator?
nodes.text: The general question the moment raises for anyone scanning for opportunities: which physically-ready hard-tech markets are frozen under an expensive certifier when a cheaper regulator already has jurisdiction over the same physics?
nodes.rationale: A generalisation one step above the episode: c6 states that regulatory arbitrage has moved from crypto into hard tech and c2 gives one worked instance, but nothing in the transcript claims the pattern repeats, so the reading is plausible and contestable rather than forced.
nodes.idea: A screen for hard-tech opportunities: enumerate categories where a cheaper certifier already has jurisdiction over the same physics, and back the teams that design to that boundary.

nodes.label: We are building flying boats
nodes.text: Flying below 150 metres, and internationally under the IMO, the craft is certified as what is technically a boat: so what they are building are flying boats.
nodes.source_quote: But if you're going through the Coast Guard, and so it's if you're flying sub 150 meters and it's the same thing internationally, you're up under the IMO, you get certified as like what is technically a boat. So what we're building are flying boats.

nodes.label: Seagull: quarter scale, 2-ton craft
nodes.text: The Seagull started as a quarter-scale prototype of a full-scale vehicle that will be 50 feet long with a two-ton capacity.
nodes.source_quote: And really the Seagull has started as like a quarter scale prototype of a full scale vehicle, which is gonna be a 50 foot, two ton capacity vehicle.

nodes.label: A third of air freight per kg-mile
nodes.text: Commercial operations start with medical deliveries to remote islands; at full scale, carrying two tons, the aim is to compete with air freight for coastal and island cargo at roughly a quarter to a third of the price per kilogram per mile.
nodes.source_quote: mostly like medical deliveries to remote islands. And then at the full scale carrying two tons, the idea is to be able to compete with air freight for coastal and island logistics and cargo and through a bunch of things we are gonna be able to get to roughly a quarter or third the price per kilogram per mile.

nodes.label: DoD mission profiles for Seagull
nodes.text: Poseidon took the Seagull to the DoD, specifically the Naval Surface Warfare Center and SOCOM, who each had their own mission profiles for a large payload in the marine domain.
nodes.source_quote: So we reached out to the DoD, specifically like the Naval Surface Warfare Center people and SOCOM, and they all had their own specifically mission profiles that they were interested in with the Seagull. So it's pretty large payload capacity relative to size and being able to operate in marine domains.

nodes.label: Design to the regulatory boundary
nodes.text: The governing thought one level up, never stated: let the certification boundary set the specification. Stay under 150 metres and inside the Coast Guard's jurisdiction, and take the cost advantage that follows.
nodes.rationale: a1 states the boundary (sub-150 metres, certified as a boat) and c2 and c3 state what the boundary is worth (a decade of FAA certification avoided), but the design rule itself - build to the regulator rather than to the mission - is never put into words.

nodes.label: Defense first, then island cargo
nodes.text: Defense is the beachhead: DoD mission profiles fund the vehicle while the commercial answer starts small with medical deliveries and scales to coastal cargo.
nodes.rationale: The founder gives defense interest as already concrete (a4) and describes the commercial programme as starting with medical deliveries before the two-ton full scale (a3); the sequencing is a reading of that ordering, not a stated strategy.
